fields.title: Polka: One Week to Release, Half the Sprint is Stalled
fields.summary: Everyone is busy, but the release is not coming together. Decide what to do in the remaining week.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do in the remaining week before the release?
fields.brief/company: Polka is an inventory app for small grocery stores. Team: four developers, one QA engineer, and you.
fields.brief/context: It is a two-week sprint, day 9. The release is next Friday, and thirty pilot stores know about it: they were promised faster scanning. There are eleven tasks in the sprint, with three in the 'Done' column.
fields.brief/objective: Release something on Friday that pilot stores can actually use, without breaking trust.
fields.brief/constraints: The team composition cannot be changed. The date can be moved, but you will have to inform the thirty stores.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do in the remaining week and explain your reasoning.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: A full board is not speed
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When everyone is busy but the release is not coming together, it is almost never about the number of hands. Work piles up before the narrowest bottleneck—review, testing, approval—and that is where all the half-done work sits, which is worth nothing until it reaches the end. The first move in this situation is not to add more, but to stop adding and clear the queue.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Done — 3.
In review — 4 (age: 5 days, 5 days, 4 days, 2 days).
In progress — 4.
Not started — 0.

Reviews are handled by a single person who is also leading the sprint's largest task — "quick scan".

There are no WIP limits on the board. Over nine days, three tasks moved to "done": two on the first day (finished from the previous sprint) and one on the seventh.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Eleven tasks. Seven have a 'high' label, four have 'medium'. The order of tasks is not defined anywhere.

Among the 'high' ones: fast scanning, discrepancy screen, cancel accidental scan, export report, dark theme, updated icons, new version banner.

Pilot stores were promised exactly one thing: faster scanning. They do not know about the rest.

The 'fast scanning' task consists of three parts: a new product search method, catalog cache, and the result screen. The first two are ready and in review, the third is in progress.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Day 4: 'doing reviews, a lot has piled up'.
Day 5: 'doing reviews and scanning'.
Day 6: 'same'.
Day 7: 'same'.
Day 8: 'finishing scanning, reviews later'.
Day 9: 'same'.

The standup format is 'what I did yesterday'. Not once in nine days did anyone mention that a task was stuck, even though three tasks on the board hadn't moved since day 5.

The QA engineer does not attend standups: 'I have nothing to say until tasks arrive'.
fields.evidenceCards/3/title: What 'Done' Means and What Was Promised
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
The team has no shared Definition of Done. In the last release, a debate on whether a task is considered done without testing on old Android devices took twenty minutes at the demo.

QA engineer: 'If all four tasks from review reach me on Thursday, I will only have time to test the happy path. I won't be able to test on a real catalog of four thousand items.'

Support specifically requests: twenty tickets a month about canceling accidental scans, promised to be fixed in this release.

Last time, no one asked the product manager what to consider a successful release; they just looked at the dashboard afterward.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Clear the review bottleneck and deliver one cohesive slice
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Stop pulling in new work, assign two people to reviews, sequence the remaining tasks, and finish only what makes up the promised faster scanning. Define release success criteria before the release.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
On day 10, two people switch to reviews, and the queue of four tasks is cleared in a day and a half. The result screen is finished by Wednesday.
Out of eleven tasks, five make it into the release: three parts of scanning, cancel accidental scan, and the discrepancy screen. The dark theme, icons, and banner move to the next sprint—no one outside knew about them anyway.
The QA engineer gets the tasks on Wednesday and manages to test them on a real store export: finds that search takes eight seconds on four thousand items. This is fixed on Thursday.
Before the release, success is defined: inventory time will drop from 90 to 70 minutes over three weeks, and the discrepancy rate will not increase.
The release goes out on Friday, and the promise is kept.
Trade-off: six out of eleven tasks are not done, and the team spent a day and a half on reviews instead of development.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Ask the team to work over the weekend
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: There are many tasks and little time. Agree on overtime to close all eleven tasks by Friday.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The team agrees. Over the weekend, they close four more tasks, all of which go to review by the same person—the queue grows to seven tasks up to eight days old.
On Thursday, the QA engineer gets everything at once and only tests the happy path. The release goes out on Friday.
On Monday, eleven support tickets come in from pilot stores: scanning freezes on catalogs with more than three thousand items. The release is rolled back.
Trade-off: you increased the amount of half-done work and added load to the exact bottleneck.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Postpone the release by two weeks
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The sprint clearly won't fit. Honestly inform the thirty stores about the delay and finish everything properly.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The delay is announced on Wednesday. The stores react calmly—most weren't prepared for a specific date anyway.
Over the two extra weeks, all eleven tasks are closed. But reviews are still done by one person, there are no WIP limits, and by the end of the new period, there are five tasks in the queue again, four days old.
The release goes out two weeks late with the same quality issues: the QA engineer gets everything in the final days again.
Trade-off: you bought time but didn't address the root cause—the workflow remained the same.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Release what is ready on Friday
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Take the three completed tasks and whatever else manages to get done, release on time, and postpone the rest. Do not move the date.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
By Friday, the three completed tasks plus two from review make it. The release goes out on time.
It includes the catalog cache and the new search method, but not the result screen—which was in progress. Faster scanning is physically in the product but inaccessible to the user: the old screen cannot display the new result.
Pilot stores don't see what was promised and write about it. You have to explain that the feature is 'almost ready'.
Trade-off: you kept the date but released a set of tasks that doesn't form a single complete user scenario.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: The queue is not ordered: priority is set by labels rather than sequentially
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The task went into progress without a discussion, and the discrepancy surfaced during acceptance
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: The deviation from the plan was visible days in advance, but no one called it out
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: The bottleneck in the flow is not identified: they look at busyness rather than task age
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: The definition of 'Done' is understood differently; the team has no shared minimum standard
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Acceptance is done by showing the happy path on test data
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: A recurring issue is addressed with text instead of removing the root cause
fields.rubric/remediation/7/gap: Release success is defined after the fact based on a rising chart
